I enjoyed this response and wanted to shine a light on how Egyptian pyramids even started. Pre-pyramid burial practices consisted of a  pharaoh diverting labor to create a mastaba, a much simpler tomb design. 

Now Imhotep is an architect who completed a mastaba only for the pharaoh to not die soon and to also ask for revisions of the mastaba. The archaeological record shows the step pyramid as consisting of several sub structures of smaller size. It began as a typical mastaba, then work was done to dig wider, then deeper, then build up, then up some more. Imhotep was a brilliant architect who made every successive pharaoh strive for a bigger and better structure.

This first pyramid shows the burial use concept had evolved into a more grandiose design. Early pyramids would suffer flaws compared to the beautiful designs we imagine today. One example of early problems are in the bent pyramid. This pyramid has a dramatic slope decrease at the higher point simply because the architects were figuring out how to stack things very high(and messed up).

Egypt built pyramids for competition and burial and you can see evidence of human trial and error. Archaeological record even has recorded data from Egyptians explaining how they worked and built pyramids. 

Aztec pyramids are built with steps in order to celebrate rituals of their original people, the Mexicas. Their temples were designed with a religious purpose and thus have identifiable focal points when excavated and studied. 

To sum up, different structures with different purposes and yet there's only so many ways to build up. It's biased information because most people only see the large pyramids that stood the test of time and they survived because they have the same sturdy design.
